reference.source: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care / Creasy and Resnik's Maternal-Fetal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Hydrops fetalis is defined by abnormal fluid accumulation in two or more foetal compartments, such as ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and generalised skin oedema
It is classified as immune (from red cell alloimmunisation) or non-immune, and non-immune causes now account for the large majority of cases
Immune hydrops results from maternal antibody-mediated haemolysis of foetal red cells, classically anti-D but also other blood group antibodies, causing severe anaemia and high-output cardiac failure

Non-immune causes are diverse and include cardiovascular anomalies and arrhythmias, chromosomal and syndromic conditions, thoracic and lymphatic malformations, congenital infection, and inherited anaemias or metabolic disease
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity on Doppler is a key non-invasive marker of foetal anaemia and guides the need for intervention
Antenatal management may include intrauterine transfusion for anaemia and treatment of foetal arrhythmia, with planned delivery in a unit able to provide intensive neonatal resuscitation
At birth the infant may need respiratory support, drainage of large effusions, correction of anaemia, and careful fluid and cardiovascular management
reference.pathophysiology: Hydrops fetalis is the end result of an imbalance between fluid movement out of the vascular space and its return, leading to interstitial fluid accumulation and effusions in multiple compartments. In immune hydrops, maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy foetal red cells, causing severe anaemia, tissue hypoxia, high-output cardiac failure, and hepatic congestion with reduced albumin synthesis. In non-immune hydrops a wide range of mechanisms converge on the same picture: heart failure from structural disease or arrhythmia, obstruction of venous or lymphatic return, hypoproteinaemia, increased capillary permeability, or severe anaemia from causes other than alloimmunisation. Raised central venous pressure, low oncotic pressure, and lymphatic dysfunction combine to drive fluid into the interstitium and body cavities.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated foetal ascites or isolated pleural effusion without generalised hydrops
Foetal or neonatal cardiac failure from structural heart disease or arrhythmia
Congenital infection such as parvovirus, cytomegalovirus, syphilis, or toxoplasmosis
Chromosomal or syndromic disorders including Turner syndrome and trisomies
Inherited anaemias such as alpha-thalassaemia major and metabolic storage disorders
additionalInvestigations: Maternal blood group and red cell antibody screen to identify alloimmunisation
Foetal ultrasound and echocardiography to define effusions, structural anomalies, and rhythm
Middle cerebral artery Doppler peak systolic velocity to assess foetal anaemia
Karyotype or microarray and, where indicated, targeted genetic and metabolic testing
Maternal and neonatal screen for congenital infection
Neonatal full blood count, blood film, bilirubin, albumin, and imaging of effusions
redFlags: Severe foetal or neonatal anaemia with signs of high-output cardiac failure
Large pleural or pericardial effusions causing respiratory or cardiovascular compromise at birth
Rapidly progressive hydrops or associated maternal mirror syndrome
Hydrops with a lethal underlying anomaly or profound multi-compartment involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends strongly on the underlying cause and gestation at presentation: immune hydrops and some treatable arrhythmias or anaemias can respond well to intrauterine and neonatal therapy, whereas hydrops from chromosomal, structural, or metabolic disease often carries a poor outcome. Overall mortality in non-immune hydrops remains high, particularly when it presents early or with a severe underlying condition.
pitfalls: Assuming an immune cause and not pursuing the broad non-immune differential when the antibody screen is negative
Failing to identify and treat a reversible cause such as a tachyarrhythmia or parvovirus anaemia
Delivering without adequate preparation for complex neonatal resuscitation and effusion drainage
Overlooking maternal mirror syndrome, which threatens maternal wellbeing
Aggressive fluid resuscitation of the neonate without recognising underlying cardiac failure
references: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care
management: Intrauterine transfusion for foetal anaemia, particularly in immune hydrops from red cell alloimmunisation, guided by middle cerebral artery Doppler
Treatment of the identified cause, including transplacental antiarrhythmic therapy for foetal tachyarrhythmia and thoraco-amniotic shunting for large effusions or thoracic lesions
Serial surveillance with foetal ultrasound, echocardiography, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
Planned delivery in a tertiary centre able to provide advanced neonatal resuscitation, including drainage of effusions, ventilation, and correction of anaemia
Neonatal exchange transfusion and phototherapy for immune haemolysis, with intensive supportive care of effusions and cardiac failure
Multidisciplinary care across foetal medicine, neonatology, cardiology, and genetics, with palliative care where the prognosis is poor
Genetic counselling and, for immune hydrops, anti-D prophylaxis and antibody management to prevent recurrence
